transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-06 10:30 PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Connor (Redwood SE), Aisha (Cerulean Head of ML), Diego (Platform), Hannah (Product)

Summary: quick discovery focused on p95 streaming latency for the logistics routing assistant. Customer wants firm numbers for hosted plan and considerations for Dedicated/Private if they need stricter SLOs and on-premise data controls.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we're on the record. Quick round-robin intros and then we'll jump into the workload profile.
[00:10] Aisha: Hi, I'm Aisha, running ML for Cerulean, we own the routing assistant model and the inference infra decisions.
[00:15] Diego: Diego, platform, I'll own integration and networking.
[00:20] Hannah: Hannah, product, focused on latency for driver-facing updates.
[00:25] Jordan: Jordan, SE at Redwood, I'll dig into performance and run the benchmarks.
[00:30] Connor: Connor, solutions eng, I'll follow up on Private/VPC specifics.

[02:10] Aisha: To lay it out, our main goal — we need to keep the driver assistant streaming fast. We show partials to drivers as new instructions come in, ideally p95 under 250ms for partial updates. That's the tight one; average can be lower but p95 matters because when it's slow drivers complain.
[02:40] Maya: Got it. Are those partial updates single-turn short outputs or multi-token streaming for longer reroutes?
[02:50] Aisha: Usually short — 20 to 80 tokens per partial, but sometimes a full reroute can be 200-400 tokens. We expect bursts when an incident hits a region, like 300 concurrent streams in a 30s window.
[03:20] Diego: Peak concurrency in production could be 600 across regions but per-region we want to size for 300-400.

[04:00] Jordan: Okay, that helps. A few clarifying Qs: what do you consider a streaming partial — do you need server-sent events style or true chunked token streaming?
[04:12] Hannah: SSE is fine, we use JS client that handles chunks; we just want the first token flow to be visible quickly.
[04:20] Jordan: Understood. For p95 at 250ms with 300 concurrent streams, there are three levers — model variant/size, batching vs immediate dispatch (continuous batching), and network locality.

[05:05] Aisha: We're evaluating Hosted first, Dedicated if we need more predictable tail latency, Private only if required for data residency. Is that a typical progression?
[05:15] Maya: Yes, most customers start Hosted for speed. Dedicated gets you reserved GPU pools and more consistent cold-start behavior; Private gives you full network control and can reduce cross-tenant variability but needs ops bandwidth.

[06:10] Diego: For Hosted, what's our expected p95 delta vs Dedicated? Any numbers ballpark?
[06:20] Jordan: Ballpark — for a medium-sized model that produces partials of 40 tokens, on Hosted in a well-provisioned region we see p95 streaming partials around 180-320ms depending on region and current load. Dedicated tightens that to 120-220ms because you control the capacity and don't share noisy neighbors. Those numbers assume our continuous KV caching and small-batch optimizations are enabled.
[06:55] Diego: So Hosted could be near 300ms p95 in worst case. That's concerning.
[07:02] Maya: Right, and we can offer reserved capacity (Dedicated) and also autoscaling windows tuned for peak events — that reduces the p95 tail.

[07:30] Hannah: What's the token/sec expectation per stream? I think we see roughly 12 tokens/sec on average, spikes to 40 when it's verbose.
[07:40] Aisha: For math, 300 streams * 12 tokens/sec = 3600 tokens/sec sustained, burst up to 12k during incidents.
[07:52] Jordan: That's helpful. We'll run a token/sec benchmark with your corpus to get real throughput numbers. Important to simulate prefix context — you said we keep a 256-token context?
[08:05] Aisha: Yes, context is 256, but we only add last 64 tokens to the request as a rolling prefix to keep latency low.

[09:00] Connor: Note on KV cache: if you have repeated prompts or similar prefixes, we can utilize prefix caching to return faster partials; but when prompts are highly dynamic that benefit shrinks. Do you have repeated patterns in the driver messages?
[09:18] Diego: Somewhat — navigation templates repeat, but incident descriptions vary. We expect modest cache hits, maybe 20–30% on some flows.

[10:00] Aisha: How do you handle batching for streaming? We can't wait 50ms to batch if it hurts initial token latency.
[10:10] Jordan: We support continuous batching — the runtime forms tiny batches without blocking initial token emission. For streaming, first token latency is prioritized; subsequent tokens are accelerated via small micro-batches. There's a configurable batching window that we can tune to your p95 target.

[12:00] Diego: Network — we're in AWS us-west-2, but some drivers hit us from central and east regions. If we use Hosted, can we pin region?
[12:12] Maya: Yes, you can select region. For strict locality we recommend Dedicated in us-west-2; Private would give you on-prem or VPC peering for the absolute lowest network variance.

[13:30] Hannah: Security check — we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS for keys, audit logs, and if Private, support for HSM.
[13:45] Connor: We have SOC2, SAML SSO, and KMS integrations. Private supports customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM and we can share audit log retention options. We'll attach the security pack.

[15:00] Aisha: Cost trade-offs — Dedicated seems expensive but maybe necessary to shave 50-100ms off tail. Is quantization or smaller model family recommended?
[15:12] Jordan: Quantization can reduce inference latency and cost but may impact output quality. For route optimization short partials, a quantized 7B variant often hits the sweet spot. We can run A/B tests against your prompts.

[17:00] Maya: Quick note — competitors came up in your RFP?
[17:05] Aisha: We looked at OpenAI for general quality and Anthropic for safety; latency variability was a concern with both. We also piloted a self-hosted stack but ops overhead was high.

[18:20] Diego: Practical question — can Redwood guarantee no cross-tenant noisy neighbor interference for Hosted?
[18:28] Jordan: We can't guarantee it like Dedicated, Hosted is multi-tenant. We do autoscaling and dynamic routing to mitigate noise, plus SLA tiers. If you need hard isolation, Dedicated is the option.

[20:00] Aisha: For benchmarks, what do you need from us?
[20:05] Jordan: A representative set of prompts (the streaming corpus), a traffic profile (concurrency over time), and a sample of context sizes. If you can provide a synthetic load pattern with peaks we can replay it on our test harness.

[21:20] Diego: We'll send a JSON file with timestamps and token counts. Also we want to see end-to-end p95 numbers including network and our client.
[21:28] Connor: We can provide an agent that runs the benchmark from your VPC to capture network time if needed. That helps separate network vs compute tail.

[23:00] Hannah: Fallback strategy — what happens if Dedicated scaled down during a spike? Do you have cross-region fallback to Hosted?
[23:12] Jordan: Yes, Redwood supports policy-based routing: failover to compatible hosted model variants in another region or fallback to a smaller cached model. That adds latency but keeps service available. We'll map your policies during PoC.

[25:40] Maya: Let's align on concrete numbers we'll try to validate: target p95 for first token partial <= 250ms, steady-state p95 for full chunk <= 450ms, sustained 4k tokens/sec with 12k tokens/sec burst. Sound right?
[25:56] Aisha: Yes. Also include tail percentile 99 for incident readiness.

[27:10] Jordan: We'll produce a benchmark plan: synthetic replay, regional runs, and Hosted vs Dedicated baseline. Expect initial results in about a week.

[28:30] Diego: Integration — for Dedicated we need to understand autoscale warm-up windows and pre-warming.
[28:38] Connor: Dedicated supports target-based prewarm and scheduled bursts; we'll document recommended policies.

[30:00] Aisha: Any gotchas around streaming SDK or client disconnects? We saw partials lost when networks flapped.
[30:10] Jordan: Our SDK supports resumable streams for short disconnects, and we can persist partials via prefix caching to reduce cost on reconnect. We'll include SDK best practices.

[33:00] Hannah: Questions from product — how fast can we iterate on model versions without impacting p95?
[33:10] Maya: We support canary rollouts and traffic weights. You can pin a percentage of traffic to new model; rollback is immediate. That lets you test without impacting overall p95 drastically.

[35:20] Aisha: If we go Private, what's the delivery timeline roughly? We may need on-prem in 3 months if compliance locks in.
[35:30] Connor: On-prem Private typically 8-12 weeks from contract for standard integrations, less if you want cloud VPC-only. We'll confirm after we see your infra.

[37:45] Diego: For the benchmark, can you run with our quantized model artifact? We have a 7B quant build we'd prefer to test.
[37:55] Jordan: Yes, we can run with your artifact in Dedicated or Private; Hosted has restrictions for custom artifacts but we can evaluate. We'll need a model package and compatibility notes.

[40:00] Maya: Recap and next steps — Jordan will run the benchmark, Maya will send pricing and security pack, Cerulean will share traffic and prompt corpus. We'll schedule a follow-up next Tuesday to review initial results.
[40:20] Aisha: Great. Please include the estimated cost for a Dedicated pool sized to hit the p95 target.

[41:10] Jordan: One more note — we'll include a small experiment to measure prefix cache hit improvement; if we can get 20% cache hits that often reduces token/sec and tail significantly.

[44:00] Hannah: Thanks all, that was useful. Looking forward to the results.
[44:15] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll send notes and artifacts after the call.

[45:00] Call ends.
